We recommend benchmarking prompt optimizers against generate-and-select controls and reporting rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs alongside accuracy. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/bhc6/DCPS.

papers.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
papers.abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

papers.title: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
papers.abstract: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.

papers.title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
papers.abstract: Modern ranking and decision systems combine components with divergent objectives, and scores calibrated at the model boundary are used as calibrated probabilities throughout the funnel, across filtering, reranking, business-rule enforcement, and auctions. Yet calibration is typically validated only where the score is produced, so its breakdown where the score is used is routinely overlooked. We ask when calibration survives this selection, how inherited error differs from selection effects, and what can fail for a perfectly calibrated score at a component boundary. We study these questions through a boundary-wise diagnostic framework of residual identities. We target rubric-judged relevance rather than presentation-dependent metrics such as CTR, so calibration is measurable at every funnel layer of interest. We first present an industry-wide case study that applies our diagnosis to settings where calibration deteriorates at decision time, tracing the degradation to selection rather than model error. This diagnosis motivates Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR): post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test, FAR cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency. We further adapt two public datasets to simulate industry settings, providing additional evidence for the mechanism. We plan to release the adapted datasets and their generation pipeline to support further research. Finally, we distill these findings into practical operating principles for calibrating multi-stage scoring systems.

papers.title: High-Fidelity Binarized Neural Vocoder
papers.abstract: Neural vocoders have achieved remarkable progress in high-fidelity waveform generation in recent years, but most existing methods still rely on full-precision operators, leading to non-negligible storage and computational costs during inference. Binary neural networks (BNNs) provide an alternative direction by quantizing weights and activations to 1 bit. However, directly applying binarization to neural vocoders is rather challenging as it inherently incurs severe information loss. To this end, we propose BiVoC, a BNN-oriented time-frequency neural vocoder for high-fidelity waveform generation. Building on our previous full-precision RNDVoC framework, BiVoC adapts the inverse-problem formulation, range-null decomposition, and fineto-coarse non-uniform subband modeling to the 1-bit setting. Specifically, we develop a simple binarized convolutional unit to provide stable time-frequency feature modeling under binary representations. Furthermore, we analyze the quality-complexity sensitivity of different modules and propose a mixed-precision design to retain quality-sensitive components in full precision while binarizing computation-dominant parts. Extensive experiments are conducted on LibriTTS and multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks. Both objective and subjective results demonstrate that BiVoC substantially outperforms BNN variants obtained by directly binarizing existing vocoders, while achieving competitive performance against several mainstream full-precision vocoder baselines under much lower theoretical computational cost. These results demonstrate the promising potential of BNNs in the audio generation field. Codes and pre-trained weights are available at https://github.com/Andong-Li-speech/BiVoC.

papers.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
papers.abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

papers.title: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable honeypots to generate responses and deceptive artefacts on demand, yet existing approaches evaluate generated content one reply at a time and leave open whether artefacts that jointly describe a coherent event retain an attacker better than unrelated ones. This question becomes pressing as autonomous LLM-driven offensive agents emerge as realistic adversaries. This paper proposes narrative deception, a reactive strategy in which the defender maps each observed attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, selects a compatible scenario from a curated catalogue based on MITRE Engage, and deploys mutually referential artefacts (files, processes, services, and logs) on an emulated Ubuntu host while the intrusion is under way. An LLM-powered defender and an autonomous LLM attacker interact through a real SSH session, and the attacker's termination policy distinguishes abandonment due to suspected deception from abandonment due to loss of interest. A campaign of 1,150 sessions compares four conditions of increasing sophistication (Static, Same-TTP, Multi-TTP, and Chain) across four open-weight attacker models, four defender models, and three attacker skill levels. Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.

papers.title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.

papers.title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yorùbá language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yorùbá. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yorùbá is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yorùbá.

papers.title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.

papers.title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
papers.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.

papers.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
papers.abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

papers.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

papers.title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
papers.abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

papers.title: Physically Admissible Generative Flow Matching for Sparse Flow Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing full fluid velocity fields from sparse, localized observations is a severely ill-posed inverse problem: most of the spatial domain remains unobserved, discrete conservation laws must hold strictly, and predictive uncertainty must be reliable. Existing generative models typically enforce physical constraints only at the terminal output or via soft penalties, leaving intermediate generative trajectories unconstrained. We introduce Feasible Subspace Consistency (FSC), a framework that preserves physical admissibility as an invariant of continuous generative dynamics: tangent-space matching confines the entire ODE trajectory to the discrete conservation manifold, while mass-orthonormal coordinates preserve the kinetic-energy metric. Sparse reconstruction then reduces to amortized posterior transport in the latent space of a frozen FSC prior, ensuring every posterior sample inherits incompressibility and boundary conditions without per-sample projection loops. We validate FSC on a periodic Kolmogorov flow, where exact spectral projection isolates path tangency and metric isometry, and a wall-bounded cylinder wake with immersed obstacles, realized via matrix-free iterative projection. FSC prevents the mode-coverage collapse induced by terminal projection (increasing mode coverage from $0.000$ to $0.790$) while eliminating high-wavenumber spectral distortion. In sparse reconstruction, amortized FSC reduces global relative error by $50\%$ and $46\%$, and sensor residuals by $63\%$ and $55\%$, relative to the unconditioned prior, while delivering calibrated, spatially heterogeneous uncertainty.

papers.title: Temporal Diffusion Models for Joint Signal-Channel Estimation under Gaussian and $α$-Stable MIMO Channels
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for learning complex data distributions and solving inverse problems. However, most diffusion models rely on the Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately represent heavy-tailed data. In this work, we study diffusion-based reconstruction under Gaussian and symmetric $α$-stable fading channels, while also exploring the benefits of using possible temporal dependence in the channel. We consider two variants: pilot-based channel-only estimation and joint image-channel recovery for MIMO systems. Our approach is based on several standard and score-based diffusion models for both Gaussian and $α$-stable distributions. We refine these models by guiding the reverse diffusion process using the observation likelihood and show how a single trained diffusion model can be reused for the location-scale family of distributions without retraining. In blind MIMO recovery, separate diffusion models are used for the image and channel, and their estimates are combined through likelihood guidance. For each setting, we compare independent and temporal reconstruction, where information from previous observations is used to improve the estimation. We show that, under a time-dependent channel model, such a temporal reconstruction improves channel estimation and the quality of the reconstructed image. Finally, we show that, for the same heavy-tailed channel data, using an $α$-stable diffusion prior provides better channel estimation and image reconstruction than using a Gaussian diffusion prior.

papers.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

papers.title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

papers.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

papers.title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
papers.abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

papers.title: DGF-Asym: Adaptive Peer Weighting for Collective Estimation under Noisy and Faulty Sensing
papers.abstract: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.

papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

papers.title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
papers.abstract: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.

papers.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
papers.abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

papers.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

papers.title: Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation of 3D Abdominal Vision-Language Model for Institution-Specific HCC Classification via Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT
papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

papers.title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
papers.abstract: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model. Thirty reference recordings cover an input corpus of eight lexical words, an alternative realization of one word, a syllable sequence, and isolated syllables. Two additional paired simulation subcorpora of sixty runs each, covering two words and one syllable sequence, assess activation reliability across neural realizations. Adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under the specified criteria, with ramp rate factors held constant. The model demonstrates how neural oscillator and ramp dynamics generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules. It complements a preceding mental-lexicon model through an ordered syllable interface. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to the acoustic extension remain further integration steps. Accessible code and synchronized visualization support inspection of the neural activation trajectories and resulting vocal-tract movements.

papers.title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.

papers.title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
papers.abstract: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

papers.title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
papers.abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.

papers.title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.

papers.title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
papers.abstract: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

papers.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

papers.title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. On Synapse, for instance, it attains a DSC of 76.57% with only 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS, confirming a favorable accuracy-efficiency balance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction with lightweight local-global feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp.

papers.title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $ρ= 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.

papers.title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
papers.abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.

papers.title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
papers.abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

papers.title: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over retrieved edges, and our pre-declared cap left three quarters of planted contradictions unretrievable, first measuring the mechanism at +0.084. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on HotpotQA documents. No other mechanism survives, and two are worse than inert: once contradictions reach the prompt, a write trust-gate and the router's provenance features each cost accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1). The gate fails structurally: poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains, against 53% of gold, so groundedness scores the lie above a truthful first mention. We release the harness, attack set, and logs, and argue that silently reconciling memory is the assumption worth abandoning.

papers.title: Sample-Aligned Decoders for Latent Generative Models
papers.abstract: Latent generative models synthesize images by decoding generated latents, yet their decoder is trained only to reconstruct encoder latents and never sees the latents it decodes at test time, so the residual errors of the generator are rendered directly into the final image. Existing remedies retrain the generator, add cost at every sampling step, or make the decoder robust to perturbed real latents, assuming that generator errors resemble such perturbations. We find that they do not. Generated latents lie on the encoder latent manifold as closely as real ones, yet follow a different distribution. The decoder should therefore be adapted to the distribution of generated latents, which raises two challenges: (1) unpaired supervision, since a generated latent has no ground-truth image, and (2) latent-space drift, since a decoder freed from paired targets forgets the latent space it must decode. We propose Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), a post-training framework that fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen generator at no inference cost. Generated-Sample Distribution Alignment matches decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space, and Encoder Anchor Preservation keeps the decoder close to the original one on encoder latents. Our analysis shows that the alignment is effective only on generated latents, where it corrects each sample in proportion to how much more often the generator produces such latents than the encoder; on encoder latents it can only work against the anchor. SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers, e.g., FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for REPA-E, complements discriminator guidance, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our code and models are available at https://torpedo2003.github.io/SAD/.

papers.title: From Ideal to Real: Integrating Language Models into Smart Home for Human-Centric IoT Safety and Security Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. However, as these devices become pervasive in critical sectors such as healthcare, transportation, and home automation, they expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that may lead to privacy breaches, data theft, and physical harm. Traditional fuzz testing methods, which often operate in simulated environments assuming ideal human decisions, fail to account for the complexities of human interactions that can influence device operations in smart homes, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences. To reveal the impact of real human decisions and discover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities, we introduce an enhanced version of IoT Fuzz for smart homes by integrating large language models to emulate human decision-making processes. Our novel approach adds a layer of realism and unpredictability to the testing environment, more accurately capturing the diverse and dynamic nature of human interactions in smart home settings.

papers.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

papers.title: How Many Training Labels Are Wrong? Auditing a Fitted Model through Gradient Allocation
papers.abstract: How many labels in a training set are wrong, and which ones? The usual answers read a held-out set or the model's outputs. A held-out reading depends on how the held-out set was drawn, and an output-based reading fails once the model has fitted its wrong labels, because the loss of a fitted wrong label is small and the prediction agrees with it. We read the answer from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. Each example, together with its label, asks the network to change in a particular way. We normalise the magnitudes of its gradient into a gradient allocation and compare it with the mean allocation of every class. An example is flagged when relabelling it as its nearest other class makes its allocation fit better than under its own label, and the share of flagged examples is the reading of the noise rate. The rule has no threshold and needs no clean data, no held-out set and no further training. After the model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of CIFAR-10N, where a feature-space margin falls to 0.79-0.84 and the loss, the gradient norm and the self-influence of an example to 0.73-0.76. On such a fitted model, readings of the noise rate from predictions or feature margins fall to 0-6% at true rates of 8-58% on CIFAR-10 with ViT-S, while the audit reads 54-96% of the true rate, and at least 93% of the examples it counts carry wrong labels. On a briefly trained model, before the wrong labels are fitted, the reading lies within 1.7 percentage points of the true noise rate on CIFAR-10 from 0% to 58% noise. Confident learning, which trains four further models, separates wrong labels about as well (AUC 0.925-0.998 against 0.900-0.995) and mostly reads the noise rate more closely, at a lower precision. An audit of 5,000 examples takes 14 to 27 seconds on one GPU.

papers.title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
papers.abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

papers.title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

papers.title: Eyes in the Update? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

papers.title: Encoding, Decodability, and Use: A Five-Layer Framework for Benchmark Measurement Audits with Evidence from UAV Intent Recognition
papers.abstract: Benchmark accuracy is routinely read as evidence that a model understands the construct the benchmark measures. We propose and instantiate on AeroIntent a five-layer framework that decomposes that reading into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour. The framework separates encoding, decodability, and use as distinct levels. In the instantiation, the observation layer is unreliable on 7 of the 20 Drone programs and floors the direct visual correlate of radial velocity at a 0.26\% scale change. The representation layer exposes two task-designed RGB features with nominal signals. RAFT flow radial bias reaches $r=+0.257$ ($p=0.030$), and bounding-box optical-flow divergence reaches $r=+0.203$ ($p=0.029$). No multi-feature readout gives a fold-mean test correlation above the cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the largest positive global out-of-sample correlation is $r=+0.080$. The decoding layer sets the MDE at $|r|=0.599$ at the multi-feature Bonferroni threshold ($α=0.00714$, power 0.80), and the observed $r=+0.080$ has power 0.00. Two injection experiments establish the MDE's condition from both sides: aligned injections are detected at or above the simulated power, and orthogonal injections are not detected. The use layer finds accuracy consistent with program memory (program-identity 0.937/0.597/0.210) and multi-region static cues. The behaviour layer is consistent with accuracy not requiring a radial-velocity readout (appearance 0.6552 vs bounding-box trajectory 0.4080, cluster-level paired $Δ=+0.2471$, $p=0.0132$).

papers.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

papers.title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
papers.abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.

papers.title: InfuseLoop: Cross-Trajectory Latent Injection for Scalable Parallel Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.

papers.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

papers.title: Proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition
papers.abstract: This document constitutes the proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition. The results of this competition of constraint solvers were presented at FLOC (Federated Logic Conference) 2026 Olympic Games, held in Lisbon, Portugal from 20th to 29th July, 2026.

papers.title: SignAligner: Dual-Granularity Span Generation for Sign Language Alignment
papers.abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting.
